introTitle: Help number New York’s subway exits
introBody: We’re asking New Yorkers and subway riders to create a proposed exit numbering system together. Throughout 2027, you’ll vote on small groups of stations across the NYC Subway and Staten Island Railway. When voting concludes, we plan to present the results to the MTA.

about: The Exit Project is an independent civic initiative with a simple idea: what if every entrance and exit in the New York City Subway and Staten Island Railway had a number? Exit numbers could make unfamiliar stations easier to navigate, help people give clearer directions, and make it easier to identify specific locations in an emergency.

Throughout 2027, we'll invite New Yorkers and other subway riders to vote on how entrances and exits should be numbered. Each week, a different group of stations will be featured. Participants can examine the entrances and exits at each station and decide which numbers make the most sense to them. At the end of the year, we'll compile the results into a comprehensive, station-by-station numbering proposal.

Our goal is to present that proposal to the MTA as both a practical starting point and a demonstration of public support for exit numbering. We can't promise the MTA will adopt the results, but we hope to make a constructive case for improving subway wayfinding. The Exit Project is entirely independent of the MTA and other government agencies. It's also completely free and non-commercial.
lifelong: Maybe you know the subway like the back of your hand. You've been using the same stations for years, and you know exactly which staircase will put you on the right corner. That's great! Exit numbers aren't intended to replace that knowledge or change how you use the subway.

But New York is a big city, and nobody knows every station equally well. Even lifelong New Yorkers occasionally find themselves somewhere unfamiliar. And, whether we like it or not, visitors and people moving to New York are part of what makes this city what it is. They deserve a subway system that's easy to navigate, too. Making things simpler for someone else doesn't make the subway any less useful to you.

There's also a practical benefit beyond convenience. In an emergency, being able to identify a particular entrance or exit could make it easier to communicate an exact location and help emergency responders coordinate. Exit numbers won't solve every wayfinding problem, but they're a relatively simple improvement that could make an already complicated system easier for everyone to use.

During open voting periods, submitted ballots are stored by the project’s Cloudflare service. Clearing browser data does not delete submitted ballots. Read the Privacy Policy for details.

paragraphs: Each week throughout 2027, we'll feature a selection of subway and Staten Island Railway stations. You'll be able to examine the entrances and exits at each station and assign numbers to them. There isn't a prescribed numbering order, so you're free to choose the arrangement that makes the most sense to you.

questions.q: What happens if I miss a week?
paragraphs: Voting takes place during each station's scheduled voting period. Once that period has ended, you won't be able to submit a vote for those stations. But don't worry! There will be plenty of other stations to vote on throughout the year.

questions.q: Why are some stations grouped together?
paragraphs: Some subway stations are connected as part of a larger station complex. When you can travel between stations without leaving the fare-controlled area, we treat them as one group for numbering purposes.
This avoids situations where different parts of the same connected complex have an Exit 1, Exit 2, and so on. Each numbered entrance or exit should be identifiable without ambiguity.
Stations connected by an out-of-station transfer are treated separately. Even when that transfer is free, passengers must leave the fare-controlled area to travel between the stations.
That means each station can have its own numbering system. For example, you might leave one station through Exit 1 and enter the next station through its own Exit 1.

questions.q: Do entrances and exits use the same numbers?
paragraphs: Yes. A numbered access point uses the same identifier whether you're entering or leaving the station.
Numbers are generally more recognizable across different languages than labels based on the English alphabet. That's particularly useful in a city as linguistically diverse as New York.

There's also a practical consideration. Some station complexes have more than 26 entrances and exits. A letter-based system would eventually need to continue beyond Z, introducing combinations such as AA, AB, and AC. Numbers provide a simpler way to handle large complexes.

questions.q: Why do subway exits need numbers?
paragraphs: Exit numbers could reduce confusion at unfamiliar stations, make directions easier to communicate, and help people identify specific entrances and exits during emergencies.
And you don't have to be new to New York to benefit from them. Even longtime residents encounter stations they don't know particularly well.
questions.linkText: Read more: But I've lived here my whole life…

questions.q: How will the voting results be used?
paragraphs: After voting concludes at the end of 2027, we'll tally the results and develop a station-by-station exit numbering proposal. We'll use the preferences expressed by voters to inform the recommended numbers.
The exact method for reconciling conflicting or closely contested assignments is still being developed.
The final report is intended for presentation to the MTA.

questions.q: Will the MTA actually implement these numbers?
paragraphs: We hope the MTA will consider the recommendations, but there's no guarantee that it will.
The Exit Project has no authority to change station signage or require the MTA to adopt a numbering system. Our aim is to offer a constructive proposal backed by public participation.

questions.q: Is the Exit Project affiliated with the MTA?
paragraphs: No. The Exit Project is an independent civic initiative and is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by the MTA or any other government agency.

questions.q: Does it cost anything to participate?
paragraphs: No. Voting is completely free. The Exit Project is non-commercial, and we're not asking for donations.

questions.q: How can I support the Exit Project?
paragraphs: The most useful thing you can do is participate! Vote when new stations become available, share the project with others, and encourage your friends and fellow subway riders to take part.
If you have suggestions or questions, visit the Feedback page linked in the site's footer.

questions.q: I've lived in New York my whole life. Why would I need exit numbers?
paragraphs: Even if you're familiar with the stations you use most often, there are hundreds of others across the subway system. Exit numbers could make navigating unfamiliar stations easier for everyone.

privacy.description: How The Exit Project handles ballots, browser storage, and external services.

sections.heading: About this policy
paragraphs: The Exit Project is an independent, non-commercial community project proposing numbers for New York City subway entrances and exits. “We” means the project maintainers. We do not collect information for advertising. This policy describes the current site, including its voting service and arrivals board.

sections.heading: Ballots and submission
paragraphs: Your ballot contains station identifiers, entrance/exit identifiers, and the numbers you assign. Drafts are saved in this browser by voting period. During an open 2027 voting period, submitting sends your ballot, a random browser identifier, and a request identifier to the project’s Cloudflare voting service. The database stores the ballot, period, receipt, request identifier, submission time, and a hash combining the period with the browser identifier. It does not store the raw browser identifier.

No account or email address is required. The voting code does not store IP addresses, hashed IP addresses, or browser fingerprints in the ballot database. One submission is accepted per browser identifier per period. This is not identity verification: another browser or cleared browser data can bypass it. Identical retries recover the same receipt. Local test mode uses a separate service and database; test votes do not count as real votes.

sections.heading: Browser storage and choices
paragraphs: The site uses localStorage under the mta-exit:v2 namespace for ballot drafts, whether you dismissed a period’s introduction, language, light/dark appearance, and background color. The arrivals board also saves station, display mode, service, platform direction, approach display, clock format, direction details, board color theme, weather toggle, and temperature unit. Some board selections can also appear in shareable URL fragments. These settings are not uploaded by the application.

The application sets no cookies and includes no analytics, advertising trackers, or CAPTCHA integrations. Its ordinary application dependencies and fonts are served with the site. External services still receive network requests as described below. Blocking localStorage prevents settings and drafts from persisting and prevents real submission; you can still explore the ballot.

For real voting, localStorage also holds a random browser identifier, request identifiers for retry recovery, and receipts. Real submission requires working localStorage. Clearing it removes these local identifiers and receipts, but does not delete a submitted ballot from the database.

sections.heading: Hosting and external requests
paragraphs: GitHub Pages hosts the site. GitHub logs and stores visitors’ IP addresses for security, including for visitors who are not signed in. This is GitHub’s processing, separate from the project’s local ballot drafts.

The voting service runs on Cloudflare Workers and stores submitted ballots in Cloudflare D1. Cloudflare receives your IP address and connection/request details. Provider request and operational logs are separate from the ballot database. The voting code does not deliberately log ballot bodies or browser identifiers. Cloudflare’s own processing is governed by its privacy policy.

Maps load tiles directly from OpenStreetMap Foundation services. Tile requests reveal your IP address, requested map areas, and browser request details, which may include a referrer. They do not contain your assigned exit numbers.

The arrivals board requests transit feeds directly from MTA servers. When weather is enabled, it requests National Weather Service data using the selected station’s coordinates, not your device location. These providers receive your IP address and request details. The app does not request device geolocation.

The separate leaflet-test.html map diagnostic page also loads Leaflet files from UNPKG, delivered through Cloudflare, and tiles from OpenStreetMap. Those providers receive connection and request details when that page is opened. The ordinary application bundles Leaflet locally.
Provider policies govern their own logs, storage, and processing; the project does not control their retention or deletion. Follow the links below for their current policies.

sections.heading: Public information and sharing
paragraphs: Station information, proposed schedules, and any built-in example results are public. The current ballot does not publish individual submissions or calculate public totals from your choices. Local drafts are not publicly visible through the site. Anyone with access to your browser profile may be able to read its saved data.
Opening external services or following links sends requests to those services. Do not put sensitive personal information in public communications or shareable links.

sections.heading: Retention, editing, and deletion
paragraphs: Local drafts, preferences, identifiers, and receipts have no automatic expiry in the application. They remain until overwritten, cleared through browser site-data controls, or removed by the browser. You can edit and reset drafts before submission. Submission does not clear the draft; an accepted real ballot cannot be edited through this interface.

Submitted ballots currently have no automatic deletion schedule. There is no self-service withdrawal or deletion feature. Clearing this site’s browser data removes local information only, may affect other projects on the same origin, and does not remove server records. Provider-held logs are subject to each provider’s procedures.

sections.heading: Security
paragraphs: We use the hosting and browser facilities available to this small project, but no website, connection, or browser storage can be guaranteed secure. Avoid using a shared browser profile for information you want to keep private.

sections.heading: Policy changes
paragraphs: We will update this page and its last-updated date when these practices change. Any future real vote collection or abuse-prevention system needs an updated explanation before use. Reading this policy or browsing the site is not explicit consent to personal-data processing.

terms.description: Terms for using The Exit Project, its ballot, maps, and community proposals.

sections.heading: Purpose and independence
paragraphs: The Exit Project is an independent, non-commercial community effort to propose NYC subway entrance and exit numbers. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the MTA or any other transit agency. You may browse, explore maps, and use the ballot for its intended community purpose.

sections.heading: Fair use and voting
paragraphs: Assign each available number once per station and complete the ballot before submitting. You can edit choices before submission. Real submissions are accepted only during the scheduled voting period and cannot be changed through this interface after acceptance. Missed periods cannot be voted in later. The browser-only limit allows one accepted ballot per browser identifier per period; it does not verify a person’s identity. Test submissions are kept separately and do not count.

Do not use automated voting, manipulate participation or results, circumvent safeguards, overload external services, or interfere with the site or other users. The maintainers may investigate suspected manipulation, exclude manipulated votes from any results, restrict abusive use, and maintain or suspend features. This does not mean that the site has a vote-monitoring or identity-verification system.

sections.heading: Community proposals, not official designations
paragraphs: Results and proposed numbers are advisory community proposals. They do not establish official MTA entrance or exit designations or require any agency to adopt them. Built-in example results are not a tally of current users’ ballots.

sections.heading: Maps and travel decisions
paragraphs: Maps, entrance inventories, accessibility details, schedules, and arrival estimates may be incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. Do not rely on this site for emergency, accessibility, or real-time operational decisions. Check official agency information, posted signs, and staff instructions for your journey.

sections.heading: Third-party services and rights
paragraphs: GitHub Pages, OpenStreetMap, MTA data services, National Weather Service services, and the separate map diagnostic page’s UNPKG delivery are provided by third parties under their applicable terms and policies. Their availability is outside the project’s control.

OpenStreetMap contributors retain rights in their data, provided under the Open Database License. Keep required map attribution and comply with applicable tile-use requirements when reusing maps. Existing content licenses, software licenses, trademarks, and other third-party rights remain in place. These terms do not claim ownership of your votes or grant rights in third-party material.

sections.heading: Availability, accuracy, and responsibility
paragraphs: The service is offered as available, without a promise of uninterrupted access, error-free information, preservation of browser drafts, or suitability for a particular purpose. To the extent permitted by applicable law, the maintainers disclaim warranties and liability for loss arising from use of, or inability to use, the site or reliance on its information. Nothing here excludes rights, warranties, or liability that applicable law does not allow to be excluded.

sections.heading: Changes to the service and terms
paragraphs: The maintainers may change, pause, or discontinue features as the project develops. Changes to these terms will appear on this page with an updated date. Review the current terms when using the service. The Privacy Policy explains current information handling separately; these terms do not turn browsing into explicit consent to personal-data processing.
